552(a)(2) now requires that all guidance originating since 1996 be made 
available electronically.® The typical agency website contains large 
amounts of guidance under an endless variety of labels, such as 
“enforcement manual,” “technical assistance manual,” “orders,” “policy 
letters,” “opinion letters,” “interpretations,” or simply “guidance.”
Because it is exempt from notice and comment, guidance is easy for 
the agency to adopt, and members of the public will often comply with 
guidance simply to avoid friction with the agency. Thus, when an agency 
feels the need to adopt a statement of general applicability (a “rule”), it is 
often tempted to do so in the form of guidance, that is, to adopt the 
statement without notice and comment and, when challenged, to argue 
that the statement is an interpretive rule or policy statement under APA 
section 553(b)(A) and therefore excepted from such procedures. But the 
courts insist that certain statements of general applicability are, by their 
very nature, legislative rules, meaning they cannot be guidance and may 
be lawfully promulgated only via APA section 553’s notice-and-comment 
procedures. Whether a statement of general applicability is by its nature a 
legislative rule (and not an interpretive rule or policy statement) is a 
question with high stakes that generates much litigation. If the answer is 
yes, the agency cannot adopt the statement without significant effort. If the 
answer is no, the agency can adopt the statement—assuming that its own 
internal review processes are not too onerous—simply by posting it on the 
internet.
We shall examine two lines of cases: those in which the agency 
contends that its statement is excepted from the notice-and-comment 
requirements for legislative rules on the ground that it is a policy 
statement; and those in which the agency contends that its statement is 
excepted from the notice-and-comment requirements for legislative rules 
on the ground that it is an interpretive rule.®
8 Section 552(a)(1)(D) requires that guidance be published (or incorporated by reference) in 
the Federal Register if it rises to the level of “statements of general policy or interpretations of 
general applicability.” But it appears that this Federal Register requirement is not much enforced. 
Russell L. Weaver, An APA I^ovision for Nonlegislative Pules?, 56 ADMIN. L. Re v . 1179, 1188 
(2004).
8 Some cases appear to elide the difference between (1) the distinction between a legislative 
rule and a policy statement and (2) the distinction between a legislative rule and an interpretive 
rule. In cases like these, it is as if there is a general category of “guidance” encompassing both 
policy statements and interpretive rules, and no need to be strict about whether an item in the 
general category is a policy statement or interpretive rule. See, e.g., Devon Energy Corp, v. 
Kempthorne, 551 F.3d 1030 (D.C. Cir. 2008). But such elision does not appear to be the norm. 
Further, several cases emphatically insist that policy statements and interpretive rules are two 
quite different things. See, e.g., Am. Mining Congress v. MSHA, 995 F.2d 1106, 1111 (D.C. Cir. 
1993); Sy neo r Int’l Corp. v. Shalala, 127 F.3d 90, 93—94 (D.C. Cir. 1997). So far as the authors have 
been able to discover, whether a court makes does or does not distinguish betw’een “policy 
statements” and “interpretive rules” has not made a difference to the outcome of an APA case.
